statement: Many species have a juvenile stage that does not reproduce.

scores.rationale: The corpus provides strong, multiple corroborating references for the existence of a non-reproducing juvenile stage. Snippet [15] is the explicit statement of the stylized fact ('Many species (almost all animals and plants) have a juvenile stage that does not reproduce'), and snippets [14] and [16] clearly define the juvenile stage in DEB theory as one where food is taken but resources are not yet allocated to reproduction. Snippets [10], [4], [5], [11], and [17] reinforce the embryo-juvenile-adult sequence with reproduction beginning only after a maturity/size/age threshold. Snippet [2] appears to contradict by allowing 'juveniles' to reproduce, but this is a simplified abstract model where the term lumps juvenile/adult together rather than genuine counter-evidence. Snippet [1] notes exceptions (precocious stoat maturity, unicellulars treated as juveniles), but these are framed as edge cases consistent with the qualifier 'many species.' Overall the evidence is clear and the consensus strongly corroborates the fact.

scores.rationale: Several snippets explicitly affirm the existence of a non-reproductive juvenile stage. Snippet 10 directly states most animals develop from juveniles that cannot reproduce to sexually mature adults, and snippet 9 explicitly distinguishes juveniles 'not yet capable of reproduction' that can only allocate to future reproduction. Others (2, 4, 5, 8, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17) reference juvenile stages, sexual maturity transitions, and delayed reproduction, consistent with the fact though more peripherally. No snippet contradicts the stylized fact. While the support is clear and uncontested, only a couple of snippets bear strongly and directly on the claim, so evidence strength is moderate; the consensus direction is clearly corroborating.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact that many species have a non-reproducing juvenile stage is strongly and repeatedly corroborated across the corpus. DEB-theoretic sources explicitly distinguish embryo, juvenile, and adult life stages with reproduction beginning only upon reaching a maturity threshold (Sous2007, Kooy2010, LikaKooy2011, van der Meer 2016), and several empirical/biological sources affirm that juveniles cannot or do not reproduce (snippet 21 on juvenile lizards, snippet 22 on C. elegans, snippet 11 on sticklebacks needing 1-2 years to mature). Snippet 2 appears to allow 'juvenile organisms can reproduce' but this is a modeling simplification merging juvenile/adult stages rather than a biological contradiction, and even it presupposes a maturity threshold. The few near-contradictory examples (e.g., the stoat reaching maturity before weaning in snippet 1) are explicitly framed as unusual variations, reinforcing the general rule. Overall the evidence is multiple, clear, and consistent with little genuine conflict.

snippets.text: rg/10.7554/eLife.43660.001 eLife digest Most animals develop from juveniles, which cannot reproduce, to sexually mature adults. The most obvious signs of this transition are changes in body shape and size. However, changes also take place in the brain that enable the animals to adapt their behavior to the demands of adulthood. For example, fully fed adult male roundworms will leave a food source to search for mates, whereas juvenile males will continue feeding. The transition to sexual maturity needs to be carefully timed. Too early, and the animal risks compromising key stages of development.

snippets.title: Preface
snippets.label: neutral
snippets.text: Sexually reproducing animals are faced with various challenges in order to find, approach and copulate with a mate in reproduction, achieve fertilisation and finally ensure that the offspring survive and in turn reproduce. In social species, this whole process includes additional dimensions involving sometimes intricate relationships of competition and cooperation; further contributing to the overall complexity. Reproduction is central to the survival of the lineage, its suppression leads to extinction.
